clue.text: The test here is to combine a short ordeal with the means of being blown up.

definitions.note: a noun in the surface, but the answer is the verb to test

indicators.note: something cut short loses its tail, so the last letter goes
to combine two things is to join them, so the pieces are set side by side

parts.note: an exam is an ordeal for the candidate who sits it

parts.words: the means of being blown up
parts.note: a buried explosive charge that blows up whoever treads on it

explanation.surface: A sadistic examiner sets candidates a brief ordeal followed by a minefield.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1930 setters still put a definition like 'The test here' at the head of the clue; 'combine' and 'with' just mean join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To examine something is to put it to the test, to inspect and try it.

clue.text: There are three of these in our realm.

definitions.text: There are three of these in our realm.

parts.note: the surface reading: some trio of things in the kingdom
the setter's reading: the phrase 'of the realm' completes the name of the three orders

explanation.walkthrough: The three estates of the realm are the Lords Spiritual, the Lords Temporal and the Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: The orders or classes of a nation that share political power, traditionally clergy, nobles and commoners.

clue.text: Not necessarily as old as the ark though it sounds as if it might be.

definitions.text: Not necessarily as old as the ark though it sounds as if it might be.

parts.words: Not necessarily as old as the ark
parts.note: the setter's reading: very old, but not as old as Noah

parts.words: though it sounds as if it might be
parts.note: the surface reading: the word's first syllable is said like Noah's vessel

explanation.walkthrough: The word begins with a sound like 'ark', so it seems to boast Noah's age.
explanation.definitionFit: Belonging to an earlier period, old-fashioned or very ancient.

clue.text: The doggy part of Kent.

parts.note: the setter's reading: the London district named after dogs, whose name begins with a word for an island
the surface reading: a county of south-east England

explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Dogs is a bend of the Thames in east London, opposite Greenwich, which was once in Kent; the setter's geography is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: An island, the word that names the London peninsula called the Isle of Dogs.

clue.text: My whole is realized when my first appears.

definitions.text: My whole is realized when my first appears.

parts.note: the setter's reading: the full word describes something finished
the surface reading is a riddle; the setter means the word's first three letters spell the finish itself

explanation.walkthrough: In the old riddle form, 'my first' is the word's start, END, and 'my whole' is the full word: things are over once the end comes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ended means finished or concluded, which is what has happened once the end arrives.

clue.text: No great shakes, yet men get paid for doing it.

definitions.text: No great shakes, yet men get paid for doing it.

parts.note: the surface reading: the idiom for something unimpressive or mediocre

parts.words: yet men get paid for doing it
parts.note: the setter's reading: stirring up gently rather than violently, and paid political stirrers make a living from it

explanation.walkthrough: 'No great shakes' is an idiom for mediocre, but read literally it is mild shaking; paid agitators stir up public feeling for a living.
explanation.definitionFit: To agitate is both to shake or stir a liquid and to campaign to stir up public unrest.

clue.text: Jurisprudence may here be jumbled but there's still point in it.

indicators.note: something jumbled is thrown into disorder, so these letters are mixed

parts.note: jurisprudence is the science of law

explanation.surface: Legal theory may be muddled, but it still has a purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' means purpose in the surface, but the answer is a tool that literally has a sharp point.
explanation.definitionFit: An awl is a pointed tool for piercing leather or wood.

clue.text: Extinct royalty.
Taken.
A popular place, yet we each have one of our own.

definitions.text: A popular place, yet we each have one of our own.

parts.note: the surface reading: somewhere everyone wants to be

parts.words: yet we each have one of our own
parts.note: the setter's reading: each person has a natural sphere where they feel most at home

explanation.walkthrough: To be 'in one's element' is to be in the surroundings that suit you best, so everyone has a different one.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's natural or favourite surroundings, where they are happiest and most effective.

clue.text: If this were present it would concern fishing.

definitions.text: If this were present it would concern fishing.

parts.note: the surface reading sounds like a thing being on hand; the setter means the present tense of the verb
the setter's reading: in the present tense the word is also the angler's gear

explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' means present tense: drop the past ending and you have the angler's word for rods, lines and hooks.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a past-tense verb meaning grappled with or confronted, while its present form names fishing equipment.

clue.text: A queen's ducal father.
Fashion is backward here.

definitions.note: a place, pointed at rather than defined

indicators.note: something backward faces the wrong way, so the word runs from its end

parts.note: a mode is a fashion or style

explanation.surface: A complaint that some place is behind the times in its clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Edom was the biblical land south of the Dead Sea; 'here' is all the definition there is.
explanation.definitionFit: Edom is the ancient kingdom of Esau's descendants, named in the Old Testament.

clue.text: Degenerate liberty.

parts.note: the setter's reading: freedom that has decayed into excess
the surface reading: simple freedom, which taken too far becomes its abuse

explanation.walkthrough: The British spelling with a C is the noun; the word also means a permit, but here it is freedom abused.
explanation.definitionFit: In the sense of licentiousness, the word means freedom pushed beyond proper restraint into excess.

clue.text: Too much French wine here, perhaps.

definitions.text: Too much French wine here, perhaps.

parts.note: the surface reading: overindulging in claret or burgundy
the setter's reading: the state you end up in, named in French

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the French adjective for drunk, the state too much wine leaves you in.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for intoxicated or tipsy.

clue.text: The skin of your teeth.

parts.note: the surface reading: the idiom for the narrowest of escapes
the setter's reading: the hard outer coating teeth really have

explanation.walkthrough: 'By the skin of your teeth' means only just, but read literally it asks for the tooth's surface layer.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard glossy coating that covers the crown of each tooth.

clue.text: Took notice.
Mind a coin (anag.)

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the old abbreviation printed after the words tells the solver outright that their letters must be rearranged

parts.note: the letters of all three words, taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to look after a coin, as if minding someone's money.
explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles printed some clues as bare anagrams with no definition; the answer is simply the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no definition; the answer names a friar of the order founded by St Dominic.

clue.text: Get the wind up and I'll move, and I'm not conceited though I may sound so.

definitions.text: Get the wind up and I'll move

indicators.note: the speaker says it only sounds like that word, so its spoken form matters, not its spelling

parts.note: a conceited person is vain, and the weathercock's word is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: A nervous but modest speaker who fidgets when frightened and denies being stuck-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get the wind up' means become scared, but literally a rising wind turns the weathercock.
explanation.definitionFit: A weather vane swings round to show the direction whenever a wind blows on it.

clue.text: A deformed aunt is seen here, much respected in the East.

indicators.note: something deformed has been twisted out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A relative, twisted out of shape, turns out to be someone revered in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: TUAN is the Malay word for sir or master, the respectful address used in colonial Malaya.
explanation.definitionFit: The Malay title is a term of respect, used for a master or gentleman in the Malay world.

clue.text: A famous Norman bishop here is associated with buried city.

definitions.note: No real definition is printed: the setter points at the answer with 'here', and the wordplay does all the work

indicators.note: two things associated are put together, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: Odo of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror
the Sumerian city excavated from the sands of Iraq in the 1920s

explanation.surface: A history lesson: a Norman prelate somehow linked with a lost city under the sand.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur was in the news when this appeared, Leonard Woolley's excavations having uncovered it in the 1920s. The clue gives no definition; the answer means a smell.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no definition; the answer is a smell or scent, of any kind.

clue.text: This habitually exceeds what is expected of a Scout.

definitions.text: This habitually exceeds what is expected of a Scout.

parts.note: the setter's reading: a thing that turns all the time, not just once

parts.words: what is expected of a Scout
parts.note: the surface reading: a Boy Scout is expected to do a good turn every day

explanation.walkthrough: The Scout promise is a good turn daily; the rod a wheel spins on does far more turns than that.
explanation.definitionFit: The rod at a wheel's centre rotates continuously whenever a vehicle is moving.

clue.text: This is a separate particular or likewise.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one single thing in a list
second meaning: the Latin adverb once used to introduce each further entry in a list or account

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin adverb meaning 'also' headed each line of old inventories and wills, which is how it became the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a single article in a list, and the Latin adverb meant also or in the same way.

clue.text: This takes the canvas.

parts.note: the surface reading: something that receives or carries a load
the setter's reading: a painter's canvas, which rests on a stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the canvas' could mean a boxer knocked down, but here it is a painter's stand.
explanation.definitionFit: The wooden frame that holds a painting upright while the artist works on it.

clue.text: This, which will suit either sex, may be said to have a diplomatic interest.

definitions.text: This, which will suit either sex, may be said to have a diplomatic interest.

parts.words: This, which will suit either sex
parts.note: the setter's reading: a first name given to boys and girls alike

parts.words: may be said to have a diplomatic interest
parts.note: the surface reading sounds like a policy; the setter means a famous diplomat bore the name

explanation.walkthrough: The likely reference is Sir Esme Howard, British ambassador in Washington until 1930, when this appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christian name, of French origin, given to both men and women.

clue.text: Clothes, in spite of being this, have fitted their wearer.

definitions.text: Clothes, in spite of being this, have fitted their wearer.

parts.words: Clothes, in spite of being this
parts.note: the surface reading suggests ill-fitting garments
the setter's reading: undersized clothes still fit a little person

explanation.walkthrough: Tiny clothes are usually a poor fit, but they suit a tiny wearer.
explanation.definitionFit: Small means little in size, the kind of garment a child or slight person can wear.

clue.text: Exactly as written.
The point is missing here and only the unedible part of the fruit remains.

definitions.text: the unedible part of the fruit

indicators.note: what is missing has been taken away, so it is removed from the word

parts.note: a pippin is a kind of apple
a pin is a point

explanation.surface: Someone has eaten the good part of the fruit and left only the core.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit' does double duty: it is the pippin apple, and with its point removed what remains is its seed. PIPPIN minus PIN is PIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A pip is the small hard seed of an apple or orange, which is not eaten.

clue.text: Some times has a pro in attendance.

definitions.text: Some times has a pro in attendance.

parts.note: the setter's reading: a Latin preposition meaning 'for each', as in so much an hour, so it goes with times
the surface reading: a professional on hand; the setter means the Latin pair used when signing for someone else

explanation.walkthrough: 'Per pro', shortened p.p., is written when signing a letter on another's behalf, so the word is accompanied by 'pro'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin preposition meaning through or for each, as in per hour or per pro.

clue.text: See the other side.
This could be timed and will make you think if you prolong it.

definitions.text: will make you think if you prolong it
definitions.note: lengthened, the answer becomes a verb meaning think deeply, so this is a cryptic hint rather than a definition

indicators.note: the word could be something else if its letters were rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something you can time, which sets you thinking if you draw it out.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is not a word on its own; add the ending -ATE and you get MEDITATE, to think.
explanation.definitionFit: Extended by three letters it becomes the verb for deep contemplation or reflection.

clue.text: Sane tiles (anag.).

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the old abbreviation printed after the words tells the solver outright that their letters must be rearranged

parts.note: the letters of both words, taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles printed some clues as bare anagrams with no definition; the answer is simply the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no definition; the answer means absolutely necessary or indispensable.

clue.text: The conveyance at the end of this gloomy place may help you out.

definitions.text: The conveyance at the end of this gloomy place may help you out.

parts.words: The conveyance at the end of this
parts.note: the setter's reading: the word ends with a public vehicle

parts.words: gloomy place may help you out
parts.note: the surface reading: a bus at the end of the line rescues you from a dismal spot

explanation.walkthrough: Erebus is the dark region of the Greek underworld, and its last three letters spell a bus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the realm of primeval darkness through which the dead pass to Hades.

clue.text: This sound is rarely heard by its maker.

definitions.text: This sound is rarely heard by its maker.

parts.note: the surface reading: some noise that its maker cannot hear

parts.words: is rarely heard by its maker
parts.note: the setter's reading: the maker is asleep while making it

explanation.definitionFit: Sleepers make this rasping breathing noise but, being asleep, seldom hear themselves do it.

clue.text: Doubtless used by Eros when he was called Cupido.

definitions.text: Doubtless used by Eros when he was called Cupido.

parts.note: the surface reading: the love god's famous weapon
the setter's reading: Cupido is his Latin name, so the weapon is named in Latin

explanation.walkthrough: Cupido is the Latin form of Cupid, so his arrow takes its Latin name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagitta is the Latin word for an arrow, Cupid's weapon of choice.

clue.text: Proverbially queen of the world.

parts.note: the setter's reading: the answer comes from a well-known saying
the surface reading: some monarch; the saying crowns public view as the ruler

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb, quoted by Pascal, says public opinion is queen of the world.
explanation.definitionFit: What people think and believe, the collective view said to rule human affairs.

clue.text: Reputedly approached, by rolling.

parts.note: the surface reading: some place one is said to reach
the setter's reading: Kipling's song has the singer 'rolling down' to this Brazilian port

explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's 'Just So' verse runs 'Roll down, roll down to Rio!', so that is how the city is reputedly approached.
explanation.definitionFit: Rio de Janeiro is the Brazilian port city the Kipling song longs to sail down to.

clue.text: Here the little dog is coming back in something like his own coat.

indicators.note: something coming back travels the opposite way, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: short for Pomeranian, a small fluffy dog

explanation.surface: A small dog trots home wearing something rather like its own shaggy fur.
explanation.walkthrough: A Pomeranian is a toy dog with a thick fluffy coat, and a mop's tangle of strands looks much like it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mop's head of loose strands resembles a shaggy dog's fur, and a tousled head of hair is also called this.

clue.text: Wind.
The impression you get from these depends on the type.

definitions.text: The impression you get from these depends on the type.

parts.words: The impression you get from these
parts.note: the surface reading: the feeling something gives you; the setter means a printed copy
the setter's reading: printing machines need metal type to print from

explanation.walkthrough: 'Impression' and 'type' sound like judging character, but both are printing terms: a copy made and the metal letters it is made from.
explanation.definitionFit: Printing machines that press inked type onto paper to make each printed copy.

clue.text: This is curable.

parts.note: the surface reading points to some illness that can be healed
the setter's reading: it can be cured as leather is, preserved by tanning or salting

explanation.walkthrough: 'Curable' suggests an illness, but curing is also how hides are preserved.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal's skin with the fur on is cured, or preserved, before it is made into leather or fur.

clue.text: A transparent mineral.
Found in the Arctic.
Festival.
This wood is windy.

parts.note: the surface reading: a forest; the setter means a woodwind instrument
the setter's reading: it is blown, so it is a wind instrument

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood' and 'windy' suggest a breezy forest; together they name an instrument of the woodwind section.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-reed instrument of the orchestra's woodwind family, played by blowing.

clue.text: Ready.
Humble.
You won't enjoy life when out of these.

definitions.text: You won't enjoy life when out of these.

parts.note: the surface reading: something miserable
the setter's reading: an idiom for feeling unwell or grumpy, being out of kinds or types

explanation.walkthrough: To be 'out of sorts' is to feel unwell or irritable.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means kinds or types, and the idiom using it describes feeling off-colour.

clue.text: You may find this bundle on either side of the Rhine.

parts.note: the setter's reading: a large wrapped bundle of goods such as cotton or hay

parts.words: on either side of the Rhine
parts.note: the surface reading sounds like river trade; the setter means the city whose French name is spelt the same, which straddles the river

explanation.walkthrough: Basel in Switzerland, called Bâle in French, sits on both banks of the Rhine.
explanation.definitionFit: A bale is a large tightly bound package of hay, wool or cotton.

clue.text: An invalid with a varied expression.

definitions.note: read as the adjective, not the noun for a sick person

parts.note: the surface reading: a sick person; the setter's reading is the adjective, not valid
the setter's reading: the same word said with its stress moved changes its meaning

explanation.walkthrough: Stressed IN-valid it is a sick person; stressed in-VAL-id it means void, which is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something null has no legal force, like a contract declared void and of no effect.

clue.text: Appropriate measures for fishermen's yarns.

parts.note: the setter's reading: a lea is a measure of length for yarn
the surface reading: tall tales; fishermen's stories are lies, and the measure is said the same way

explanation.walkthrough: A lea is a textile measure of yarn, and fishermen's yarns, their tall stories, are 'lies', which sounds alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Leas are units of length for spun thread, fitting since tall tales are called yarns.

clue.text: It enters backwards at the very middle of the day, that's the idea.

indicators.note: going backwards means the word is read from its last letter to its first
something that enters goes inside, so it sits within the other piece

parts.words: the very middle of the day
parts.note: midday, the exact middle of the day
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something slips in backwards at exactly midday, and that is the whole plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The very middle of the day' is midday itself, and 'at the very middle' also says where the reversed word goes: dead centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is a thought or conception, the same as an idea.

clue.text: Satire may put you on your "metal" here.

parts.note: the setter's reading: the word for satire is this metal with 'you', the letter Y, put on the end
the surface reading is the idiom 'put you on your mettle', punned on metal

explanation.walkthrough: Satire is irony, which is this metal with Y, sounding like 'you', put on.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong grey metal, the commonest used for tools and machinery.

clue.text: This seems to imply three-fold schism.

definitions.text: This seems to imply three-fold schism.

parts.note: the setter's reading: the word's parts look like they mean something else
the surface reading: a church split three ways, as if into three sects

explanation.walkthrough: The word looks like 'tri' (three) plus 'sect' (a breakaway group), but it means cut into three equal parts.
explanation.definitionFit: To divide an angle or line into three equal parts, as geometry uses the term.

clue.text: "We … hae paidl't in the burn."

parts.note: the setter's reading: the dots mark the missing word to supply
the surface reading: a line from Burns's 'Auld Lang Syne'

explanation.walkthrough: Burns wrote 'We twa hae paidl'd in the burn': we two have paddled in the stream. A burn is a Scottish brook.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scots word for two, used throughout Burns's song of old friendship.

clue.text: An ornamental church screen.
A description of you may be broadcast if you get this, but you won't remember it.

definitions.text: A description of you may be broadcast if you get this, but you won't remember it.

parts.words: A description of you may be broadcast if you get this
parts.note: the surface reading: some misfortune that puts you on the wireless; police broadcast details of missing persons
the setter's reading: the condition is itself loss of memory

explanation.walkthrough: In 1930 the BBC broadcast police appeals describing people who had wandered off with lost memories.
explanation.definitionFit: Amnesia is loss of memory, so the sufferer cannot recall even having it.

clue.text: You might meet them in a castle in Spain.

definitions.text: You might meet them in a castle in Spain.

parts.note: the surface reading: people encountered in a daydream
the setter's reading: a castle in Spain is an idle dream, but a real Spanish castle would house Spanish ladies

explanation.walkthrough: A castle in Spain is a daydream; taken literally, its residents would be Spanish married women.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish women, addressed by the title equivalent to Mrs or madam.
